items.title: Building California School Trends
items.label: Small Web
items.excerpt:
We're trying to buy a house in one of the highest cost of living areas of the United States, and the schools aren't even good.

One thing we'd hear was "wealthier people are moving in who care about education, so this lower-performing school will improve". But was that true? How could we figure that out?

I ended up building California School Trends to solve for the problem.

Certain websites like Great Schools or Niche will show you their custom score, but it usually obfuscates the underlying fundamentals. Certain schools end up with a 7/10 that have top-decile test scores. Other schools with pretty mediocre test scores had a 9/10. Why? It was hard to tell. Were they trending up? Down? It was difficult to find out.

I ended up finding Page Turner, a non-profit that focuses on k-2nd grade reading proficiency. They had some pretty great stats, but only for reading proficiency, and it was a bit challenging to navigate their website.

items.title: Agent Experience: The Third Reader of Everything You Build
items.label: Small Web
items.excerpt:
Watch a coding agent work for ten minutes in a repository it has never seen, and count the guesses: which command runs the tests, whether the linter’s complaint is fatal, what the deployment tool means by two paragraphs of prose and a stack trace, which of the three services called billing the ticket is about, and whether the README is still true. Each guess costs tokens and time, some are wrong, and the wrong ones end up in a pull request.

Hardly any of those guesses say something about the model. They come from the system the agent was dropped into, and most of them can be designed away. How well a system serves the agents that now do much of its work has become a design concern of its own, and this post is my attempt to describe it.

The developer moved up a level

In Almost Irrelevant I argued that once agents write most of the code, the choice of programming language matters much less than it did, because the agent absorbs the learning curve, the ceremony and the boilerplate…

items.title: Designing Memory for Research Agents: Four Patterns You Can Implement
items.label: Small Web
items.excerpt:
Imagine asking a research agent when a fictional API raised its batch limit from 100 to 250 items. The agent finds an older manual and a newer release note. After dozens of tool calls, can it still explain which limit applied in April, which applies today, and where each number came from? Can it do that after the run is interrupted and resumed?

That example calls for four kinds of memory. The agent needs a working memory for the next decision, an episodic memory of what it tried, a semantic memory of what the evidence supports, and a procedural memory for how to check it. Start with a project directory and make each kind of memory responsible for a different job.

The CoALA framework separates working memory from three kinds of long-term memory. For a research agent, the distinction determines what to save, when to load it, and how to update it. Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents

Two pieces of infrastructure support these patterns. A checkpoint captures enough execution…

items.title: Playing to win
items.label: Blogs
items.excerpt:
🫧 Open on Bubbles

As I’ve written about before , every Monday night at 9pm I play pickup soccer with the same group of guys. The games and the gameplay are always different — it depends on who’s there, what the teams are, and who’s “on” that night.

When the other team has the ball, there are two main tactics. The safe option is to defend your half of the field — let them carry the ball to the halfway line before you start pressing. The more aggressive approach is a “high press”, where you try to win the ball back in the other team’s end. If you succeed, you’ve got the ball near your opponents’ goal, with most of their players out of position. If you fail, you let the other team attack while you’re out of position.

I like to play the high press. When it works, it’s just so much fun .

items.title: I Get Bored of Everything
items.label: Blogs
items.excerpt:
I’ve come to see it as a feature, not a bug.

Hobbies, friends, religion—could be ten days or ten years, but I’ll inevitably move on. I just get restless. I can feel it happening when the fervor fades. It’s like a fire goes out. A mental chill settles in.

I used to feel bad about it, like something was wrong with me. I would be hesitant to share new passions with people, fearing contemptuous sighs and rolling eyes. The inevitable comments like, Yeah, we’ll see how long this lasts.

But now that I’m older, I think, who fucking cares? For one, life is so damn short and fast. It feels like just yesterday I was walking across campus to a girlfriend’s apartment. Slightly buzzed and smoking a cigarette. Blessed with luck and immortality.

Suddenly I’m balding, my back goes out when I sneeze, and I regularly check my credit score.

But more importantly, this quirk has saved my ass. I can’t even stick with a vice. Drinking? I get tired of it and drop it altogether for months to years at a…

Do you need to leave your hometown to love it? Are some hometowns just objectively shittier than others? My hometown of Oshawa, Ontario, has left me with some thoughts on all of this.

I grew up in Oshawa in the early 2000s and spent my angsty teenage years in a suburban daze in the city's north end. My days were spent skateboarding in parking lots, loitering in McDonald's and Tim Hortons late at night, and getting into the kind of shenanigans typical of kids with little supervision (climbing buildings, drinking in basements, and occasionally throwing snowballs at cars). items.title: Preparing the earth for a persimmon tree
items.label: Q&A
items.excerpt:
I have an enormous aloe plant (about 6 feet tall, 5 feet across) that we are taking out and replacing with a persimmon tree. I'm wondering if there is something we should do between the aloe coming out and the tree going in to prepare the earth to make the tree more likely to succeed.

Given the size of the aloe, I'm expecting that it'll have a pretty big root structure that we won't be able to get access to (there is cement around 1/2 of the planting area). We have chickens and could set them up in the spot to turn over the earth after the aloe comes out. We could add compost, plant a temporary cover crop, just let it rest for a season to give the roots time to decompose, or just put the persimmon tree in right away and hope for the best.

Where I live doesn't hit freezing, but does get a lot of rain in the winter.

Any thoughts on how to prepare the earth for the new tree?
